```{r setup}
#| warning: false
library(keras3)
use_backend("tensorflow")
set.seed(123)

data <- readRDS("handwriting.rds")
meta <- data$metadata

# Pixel matrix (one row per image) used by the baselines and EDA
X <- matrix(data$images, nrow = 25000) / 255
```

# 1. Data overview

```{r}
dim(data$images)                       # 25000 x 28 x 28 x 1
data$description
range(data$images)                     # 0-255, so we scale by 255
head(meta)
table(meta$person_id, meta$session)    # 250 images per writer per session
```

# 2. Exploratory analysis

## 2.1 One digit, four writers, five sessions

```{r}
#| fig-height: 6
d <- 2
par(mfrow = c(4, 5), mar = c(0.5, 0.5, 1, 0.5))
for (p in 1:4) {
  for (s in 1:5) {
    i <- which(meta$person_id == p & meta$digit == d & meta$session == s)[1]
    image(t(data$images[i,,,1])[, 28:1], axes = FALSE, col = gray.colors(256),
          main = paste("person", p, "session", s))
  }
}
```

## 2.2 What varies: writer, session or digit?

Simple summaries per image (height, width, centre of mass), then the share of
variance explained by each factor.

```{r}
#Building the features

img  <- data$images[,,,1] / 255
feat <- t(apply(img, 1, function(m) {
  on <- m > 0.3
  r  <- which(rowSums(on) > 0)
  cc <- which(colSums(on) > 0)
  c(h = diff(range(r)) + 1, w = diff(range(cc)) + 1,
    cx = sum(m * col(m)) / sum(m), cy = sum(m * row(m)) / sum(m))
}))

#Preparing for analysis

df <- data.frame(meta, feat)
df[c("person_id", "session", "digit")] <- lapply(df[c("person_id", "session", "digit")], factor)

#Variance decomposition
for (v in c("h", "w", "cx", "cy")) {
  ss <- summary(aov(reformulate("digit + person_id + session + person_id:session", v),
                    data = df))[[1]]
  cat("\n", v, "\n")
  print(round(100 * ss[["Sum Sq"]] / sum(ss[["Sum Sq"]]), 1) |>
          setNames(trimws(rownames(ss))))
}
```
Each row is one measurement taken on every image, and each column is a possible source of variation. The numbers are the percentage of that measurement’s total variation explained by each source, so every row adds to 100.

The four measurements

h: height of the digit in pixels
w: width of the digit
cx: horizontal position of the ink (left to right)
cy: vertical position of the ink (top to bottom)

The five sources

digit: variation because a 0 looks different from a 1, 2, 3 or 4
person_id: variation because different writers write differently
session: variation because of the recording session, the same for everyone
person_id:session: variation because a particular writer wrote differently in a particular session
Residuals: the leftover variation between replicates in the same writer-digit-session

Reading each row

h (height): 62.9% is person. Writers differ mainly in how tall they write, and a writer’s height hardly changes between sessions (only 2.9%). Height is a stable signature.
w (width): it’s split between digit (43.5%, since a 1 is narrow and a 0 is wide) and person (40.5%). Writers differ in width too, and again sessions add little (6.8%).
cx (horizontal position): digit 31.6% and person 34.4%, so where a writer places the digit sideways is fairly consistent. Session × person is larger here (10.3%).
cy (vertical position): this is the odd one. Person is only 10.3%, but person × session is 17.0% and residuals are 57.3%. A writer’s vertical placement shifts from session to session and from image to image, so it is a poor feature for identifying writers.

What the table says overall

The session column is under 1% everywhere. No session is shifted for everyone, so session 4 isn’t an unusual session. This supports treating sessions as interchangeable groupings.
Person is large for height, width and horizontal position. Writers differ in measurable ways, and these differences hold across sessions.
Person × session is small for height and width, larger for cx and cy. Handwriting shifts between sessions mostly in position, much less in size.
Residuals show replicate noise. Large for cy (57%), small for w (9%).



## 2.3 Do a writer's sessions look alike?

Average image per writer x digit x session (sessions 1-4 only), then compare
distances between cells.

"how different do two handwriting samples look, depending on whether they come from the same writer or the same session?"

```{r}
dist_table <- function(M) {
  d4  <- meta$session %in% 1:4
  key <- with(meta[d4, ], paste(person_id, digit, session))
  Cm  <- rowsum(M[d4, ], key) / 50
  k   <- do.call(rbind, strsplit(rownames(Cm), " "))
  info <- data.frame(p = k[,1], d = k[,2], s = k[,3])
  #Splits the labels back into columns (writer, digit, session) so each average image can be identified.
  sapply(0:4, function(dd) {
    i <- which(info$d == dd)
    D <- as.matrix(dist(Cm[i, ]))
    a <- info[i, ]
    #For each digit separately (so a 2 is only compared with a 2), pick that digit’s 80 cells (20 writers ×       4 sessions). dist() computes the Euclidean distance between every pair of average images, and D is the       resulting 80 × 80 table of distances.
    up <- upper.tri(D)
    sp <- outer(a$p, a$p, "==")
    ss <- outer(a$s, a$s, "==")
    c(same_writer_diff_session = mean(D[up & sp & !ss]),
      diff_writer_same_session = mean(D[up & !sp & ss]),
      diff_writer_diff_session = mean(D[up & !sp & !ss]))
  })
}
dtab <- dist_table(X)
colnames(dtab) <- paste("digit", 0:4)
round(dtab, 2)
round(dtab["same_writer_diff_session", ] / dtab["diff_writer_diff_session", ], 2)
```
Distances are in pixel units, so the absolute numbers mean little. What matters is how the rows compare.

Same writer, different session (about 6.4-7.1) is smaller than different writer (about 7.9-8.8). So a writer’s handwriting is on average closer to their own other sessions than to other people’s. That’s the signal that makes any writer recognition possible.
But only a bit smaller. The ratio is 0.80, 0.83, 0.81, 0.81 and 0.80. A writer’s average digit changes between sessions by about 80% of the distance to a different writer’s digit. The gap between “my own handwriting next week” and “someone else’s handwriting” is small.
The ratio is almost the same for all five digits, so this isn’t a quirk of one digit.
Rows 2 and 3 are practically identical (8.78 vs 8.79, and so on). Different writers are no closer to each other in the same session than in different sessions. So there’s no shared session effect: sessions don’t shift everyone in the same direction. That agrees with the variance table, where session explained under 1%, and it supports treating sessions as interchangeable and holding one out.


A writer’s average digit changed between sessions by about 80% of the distance to another writer’s digit, so writer identity is only moderately more stable than session-to-session variation. Different writers were equally far apart within and between sessions, indicating no shared session effect.




# 3. Train / validation / test split (by session)

Images within a writer-session are near-duplicates, so we split by session:
sessions 1-3 train, session 4 validation, session 5 test (used once, at the end).

```{r}
tr <- meta$session %in% 1:3
va <- meta$session == 4
te <- meta$session == 5

x_train <- data$images[tr,,,,drop = FALSE] / 255
x_val   <- data$images[va,,,,drop = FALSE] / 255
x_test  <- data$images[te,,,,drop = FALSE] / 255

person_f <- factor(meta$person_id)
y_all    <- as.integer(person_f) - 1          # 0..19
n_people <- nlevels(person_f)

y_train <- to_categorical(y_all[tr], n_people)
y_val   <- to_categorical(y_all[va], n_people)
y_test  <- to_categorical(y_all[te], n_people)

dim(x_train); dim(x_val); dim(x_test)
table(meta$person_id[tr])[1:3]     # 750 per writer
table(meta$person_id[te])[1:3]     # 250 per writer
```




# 4. Baselines (validation accuracy, session 4)

```{r}
# Baseline 1: nearest centroid, using each writer's average image for the same digit
centroid_acc <- function(train_idx, val_idx) {
  pred <- integer(sum(val_idx))
  Xv <- X[val_idx, ]
  dv <- meta$digit[val_idx]
  for (d in 0:4) {
    it <- train_idx & meta$digit == d
    Cd <- rowsum(X[it, ], meta$person_id[it]) / (sum(it) / n_people)   # mean image per writer
    iv <- which(dv == d)
    d2 <- outer(rowSums(Xv[iv, ]^2), rep(1, nrow(Cd))) - 2 * Xv[iv, ] %*% t(Cd) +
          outer(rep(1, length(iv)), rowSums(Cd^2))
    pred[iv] <- as.integer(rownames(Cd))[max.col(-d2)]
  }
  mean(pred == meta$person_id[val_idx])
}
centroid_acc(tr, va)
set_random_seed(123)
# Baseline 2: linear softmax on raw pixels (no hidden layer)
lin <- keras_model_sequential(input_shape = c(28, 28, 1)) %>%
  layer_flatten() %>%
  layer_dense(n_people, activation = "softmax")
lin %>% compile(loss = "categorical_crossentropy",
                optimizer = optimizer_adam(learning_rate = 0.00010),
                metrics = "accuracy")
h_lin <- lin %>% fit(x_train, y_train, epochs = 20, batch_size = 64,
                     validation_data = list(x_val, y_val), verbose = 0)
tail(h_lin$metrics$val_accuracy, 1)
plot(h_lin$metrics$val_accuracy, type = "l", xlab = "epoch", ylab = "validation accuracy")
plot(h_lin$metrics$val_loss, type = "l", xlab = "epoch", ylab = "validation cross-entropy")

# 5. CNN models
#Base model with defaults
```{r}
compile_model <- function(model, lr) {
  model %>% compile(loss = "categorical_crossentropy",
                    optimizer = optimizer_adam(learning_rate = lr),
                    metrics = "accuracy")
  model
}

# One architecture for both models: two conv layers (relu), max pooling,
# flatten, softmax output. nu is the L2 weight penalty (nu = 0 means none).
build_cnn <- function(nu = 0, act = "relu", drop = 0.2, lr = 0.01) {
  input <- layer_input(shape = c(28, 28, 1))
  output <- input %>%
    layer_conv_2d(filters = 16, kernel_size = c(3, 3),
                  kernel_regularizer = regularizer_l2(nu)) %>%
    layer_activation(act) %>%
    layer_dropout(rate = drop) %>%
    layer_conv_2d(filters = 16, kernel_size = c(3, 3), activation = act,
                  kernel_regularizer = regularizer_l2(nu)) %>%
    layer_max_pooling_2d(pool_size = c(2, 2)) %>%
    layer_flatten() %>%
    layer_dense(units = n_people, activation = "softmax",
                kernel_regularizer = regularizer_l2(nu))
  compile_model(keras_model(input, output), lr = lr)
}

# Lecture-style CNN: no weight penalty
set_random_seed(123)
cnn_base <- build_cnn(nu = 0)
summary(cnn_base)
```

```{r}
# =====================================================================
# CHUNK 0: updated build_cnn (replace base model with default values)
# filters, kernel and pool are now arguments.
# =====================================================================
build_cnn <- function(nu = 0, act = "relu", drop = 0.2, lr = 0.01,
                      filters = 16, kernel = 3, pool = 2) {
  input <- layer_input(shape = c(28, 28, 1))
  output <- input %>%
    layer_conv_2d(filters = filters, kernel_size = c(kernel, kernel),
                  kernel_regularizer = regularizer_l2(nu)) %>%
    layer_activation(act) %>%
    layer_dropout(rate = drop) %>%
    layer_conv_2d(filters = filters, kernel_size = c(kernel, kernel), activation = act,
                  kernel_regularizer = regularizer_l2(nu)) %>%
    layer_max_pooling_2d(pool_size = c(pool, pool)) %>%
    layer_flatten() %>%
    layer_dense(units = n_people, activation = "softmax",
                kernel_regularizer = regularizer_l2(nu))
  compile_model(keras_model(input, output), lr = lr)
}


# =====================================================================
# CHUNK 1 (STAGE 1): activation x learning rate x dropout, with nu = 0
# 2 x 6 x 6 = 72 combinations, 3 seeds each = 216 fits
# =====================================================================
y_val_idx <- y_all[va]

grid <- expand.grid(act  = c("tanh", "relu"),
                    lr   = c(0.003, 0.001, 0.0003, 0.0001, 0.00003, 0.00001),
                    drop = c(0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.5, 0.6, 0.7),
                    stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
seeds <- c(123, 1, 2)

run_one <- function(act, lr, drop, seed) {
  set_random_seed(seed)
  m <- build_cnn(nu = 0, act = act, lr = lr, drop = drop)
  h <- m %>% fit(x_train, y_train, epochs = 10, batch_size = 64,
                 validation_data = list(x_val, y_val), verbose = 0)
  p <- pmax(predict(m, x_val, verbose = 0), 1e-12)
  c(train_acc = tail(h$metrics$accuracy, 1),
    val_acc   = tail(h$metrics$val_accuracy, 1),
    val_ce    = -mean(log(p[cbind(seq_along(y_val_idx), y_val_idx + 1)])))
}

grid_res <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_len(nrow(grid)), function(g) {
  cat("fit", g, "of", nrow(grid), "\n")
  r <- sapply(seeds, function(s) run_one(grid$act[g], grid$lr[g], grid$drop[g], s))
  data.frame(grid[g, ],
             train_acc = mean(r["train_acc", ]),
             val_acc   = mean(r["val_acc", ]),
             acc_sd    = sd(r["val_acc", ]),
             val_ce    = mean(r["val_ce", ]),
             ce_sd     = sd(r["val_ce", ]))
}))

# Drop collapsed runs (accuracy near chance), rank the rest by validation cross-entropy
ok1 <- subset(grid_res, val_acc > 0.10)
show <- ok1[order(ok1$val_ce), ]
show$lr <- format(show$lr, scientific = FALSE)        # keeps small rates visible
show[sapply(show, is.numeric)] <- round(show[sapply(show, is.numeric)], 3)
head(show, 10)

top <- max(ok1$val_acc)
for (tol in c(0.01, 0.02, 0.03, 0.04)) {
  near <- subset(ok1, val_acc >= top - tol)
  w <- near[which.min(near$val_ce), ]
  cat("tol", tol, ":", w$act, format(w$lr, scientific = FALSE), "drop", w$drop,
      " acc", round(w$val_acc, 3), " ce", round(w$val_ce, 3), "\n")
}

# equal-weight rank sum, for comparison
#r <- rank(-ok1$val_acc) + rank(ok1$val_ce)
#ok1[order(r, ok1$val_ce), ][1:5, c("act", "lr", "drop", "val_acc", "val_ce")]



r      <- rank(-ok1$val_acc) + rank(ok1$val_ce)
ranked <- ok1[order(r, ok1$val_ce), ]
best1  <- ranked[1, ]
best1[, c("act", "lr", "drop", "val_acc", "val_ce")]
str(best1$lr)       

```

# =====================================================================
# CHUNK 2 (STAGE 2): filters x kernel x pool, on the Stage 1 winner
# 3 x 2 x 2 = 12 combinations, 3 seeds each = 36 fits
# =====================================================================
tol_ce <- 0.30      # tolerance of 30% above best val_ce
arch_grid <- expand.grid(filters = c(8, 16, 32),
                         kernel  = c(3, 5),
                         pool    = c(2, 3))

run_arch <- function(filters, kernel, pool, seed) {
  set_random_seed(seed)
  m <- build_cnn(nu = 0, act = best1$act, lr = best1$lr, drop = best1$drop,
                 filters = filters, kernel = kernel, pool = pool)
  h <- m %>% fit(x_train, y_train, epochs = 10, batch_size = 64,
                 validation_data = list(x_val, y_val), verbose = 0)
  p <- pmax(predict(m, x_val, verbose = 0), 1e-12)
  c(train_acc = tail(h$metrics$accuracy, 1),
    val_acc   = tail(h$metrics$val_accuracy, 1),
    val_ce    = -mean(log(p[cbind(seq_along(y_val_idx), y_val_idx + 1)])))
}

arch_res <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_len(nrow(arch_grid)), function(g) {
  cat("fit", g, "of", nrow(arch_grid), "\n")
  r <- sapply(seeds, function(s)
    run_arch(arch_grid$filters[g], arch_grid$kernel[g], arch_grid$pool[g], s))
  data.frame(arch_grid[g, ],
             train_acc = mean(r["train_acc", ]),
             val_acc   = mean(r["val_acc", ]),
             acc_sd    = sd(r["val_acc", ]),
             val_ce    = mean(r["val_ce", ]),
             ce_sd     = sd(r["val_ce", ]))
}))

Checking epochs on the best model based on tuning

```{r}
nu_sel <- 0          # set to the 0 for now
n_ep   <- 60

curves <- lapply(seeds, function(s) {
  set_random_seed(s)
  m <- build_cnn(nu = nu_sel, act = best1$act, lr = best1$lr, drop = best1$drop,
                 filters = best2$filters, kernel = best2$kernel, pool = best2$pool)
  out <- matrix(NA, n_ep, 3,
                dimnames = list(NULL, c("train_acc", "val_acc", "val_ce")))
  for (e in 1:n_ep) {
    h <- m %>% fit(x_train, y_train, epochs = 1, batch_size = 64, verbose = 0)
    p <- pmax(predict(m, x_val, verbose = 0), 1e-12)
    out[e, ] <- c(h$metrics$accuracy,
                  mean(max.col(p) - 1 == y_val_idx),
                  -mean(log(p[cbind(seq_along(y_val_idx), y_val_idx + 1)])))
  }
  out
})
avg <- Reduce(`+`, curves) / length(curves)

# Same trade-off rule as the other stages: among epochs whose cross-entropy is within
# the tolerance of the minimum, take the one with the highest validation accuracy.
if (!exists("tol_ce")) tol_ce <- 0.30
e_ce     <- which.min(avg[, "val_ce"])
ok_ep    <- which(avg[, "val_ce"] <= avg[e_ce, "val_ce"] * (1 + tol_ce))
n_epochs <- ok_ep[which.max(avg[ok_ep, "val_acc"])]

par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
matplot(avg[, c("train_acc", "val_acc")], type = "l", lty = 1, lwd = 2,
        xlab = "epoch", ylab = "accuracy")
legend("bottomright", c("train", "val"), col = 1:2, lty = 1)
abline(v = n_epochs, lty = 2)
plot(avg[, "val_ce"], type = "l", lwd = 2, xlab = "epoch", ylab = "validation cross-entropy")
abline(v = c(e_ce, n_epochs), lty = 2)

c(min_ce_epoch = e_ce, chosen_epochs = n_epochs)

```


#choose nu by validation accuracy

```{r}
n_epochs <- 10
nus <- c(0, 1e-4, 1e-3, 3e-3, 1e-2, 3e-2, 1e-1, 3e-1)
y_val_idx <- y_all[va]

run_nu <- function(nu, seed) {
  set_random_seed(seed)
  m <- build_cnn(nu = nu, act = best1$act, lr = best1$lr, drop = best1$drop,
                 filters = best2$filters, kernel = best2$kernel, pool = best2$pool)
  h <- m %>% fit(x_train, y_train, epochs = n_epochs, batch_size = 64, verbose = 0)
  p <- pmax(predict(m, x_val, verbose = 0), 1e-12)            # CE computed without the penalty
  c(train_acc = tail(h$metrics$accuracy, 1),
    val_acc   = mean(max.col(p) - 1 == y_val_idx),
    val_ce    = -mean(log(p[cbind(seq_along(y_val_idx), y_val_idx + 1)])))
}

nu_res <- do.call(rbind, lapply(nus, function(nu) {
  cat("nu =", nu, "\n")
  r <- sapply(seeds, function(s) run_nu(nu, s))
  data.frame(nu = nu,
             train_acc = mean(r["train_acc", ]),
             val_acc   = mean(r["val_acc", ]),
             acc_sd    = sd(r["val_acc", ]),
             val_ce    = mean(r["val_ce", ]),
             ce_sd     = sd(r["val_ce", ]))
}))


wh <- which.min(nu_res$val_ce)
nu_final              <- nus[wh]                              # minimum validation CE
nu_final_conservative <- nus[min(wh + 1, length(nus))]        # course's "next larger nu"
nu_sel <- nu_final                                            # or nu_final_conservative

nu_res[wh, ]                                                  # check accuracy and sd at the minimum
c(best = nu_final, conservative = nu_final_conservative)

show_nu <- nu_res
show_nu[-1] <- round(show_nu[-1], 3)
show_nu

# ok_nu   <- subset(nu_res, val_acc > 0.10)
# near_nu <- subset(ok_nu, val_ce <= min(ok_nu$val_ce) * (1 + tol_ce))
# near_nu <- near_nu[order(-near_nu$val_acc, near_nu$val_ce), ]
#

# show_nu                                         # the full table
# near_nu$nu                                      # the candidates inside the tolerance
# 
# best_nu <- near_nu[1, ]
# nu_sel  <- best_nu$nu
# nu_sel

par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot(nu_res$val_ce, type = "b", pch = 16, xaxt = "n",
     xlab = "nu", ylab = "validation cross-entropy")
axis(1, at = seq_along(nus), labels = nus)
abline(v = which(nus == nu_sel), lty = 2)
plot(nu_res$val_acc, type = "b", pch = 16, xaxt = "n",
     xlab = "nu", ylab = "validation accuracy")
axis(1, at = seq_along(nus), labels = nus)
abline(v = which(nus == nu_sel), lty = 2)

#regularised mode

```{r}

# Tuned model: settings chosen on the validation session (session 4).
# act, lr, dropout from Stage 1 (best1) then filters, kernel, pool from Stage 2 (best2)

nu_reg <- nu_final_conservative 
#best validation accuracy and lowest validation error

set_random_seed(123)
cnn_reg <- build_cnn(nu = nu_reg,
                     act = best1$act, lr = best1$lr, drop = best1$drop,
                     filters = best2$filters, kernel = best2$kernel, pool = best2$pool)
summary(cnn_reg)

```

## 5.1 Train both (fixed number of epochs, validation on session 4)

```{r}
h_base <- cnn_base %>% fit(x_train, y_train, epochs = n_epochs, batch_size = 64,
                           validation_data = list(x_val, y_val), verbose = 0)
h_reg  <- cnn_reg %>% fit(x_train, y_train, epochs = n_epochs, batch_size = 64,
                          validation_data = list(x_val, y_val), verbose = 0)

plot(h_base)
plot(h_reg)

c(base_train = tail(h_base$metrics$accuracy, 1),
  base_val   = tail(h_base$metrics$val_accuracy, 1),
  reg_train  = tail(h_reg$metrics$accuracy, 1),
  reg_val    = tail(h_reg$metrics$val_accuracy, 1))
```

# 6. Final evaluation (session 5, used once)

Choose the model with the better validation accuracy and put it in `final`.
Differences of a few points are within noise (see the report text), so prefer
the simpler or less overfit model when they are close.

```{r}
final <- cnn_reg     # <- change to cnn_base if it validated better

model_acc <- function(model, x, y_idx) {
  hat <- max.col(predict(model, x, verbose = 0)) - 1
  list(hat = hat, acc = mean(hat == y_idx))
}

res <- model_acc(final, x_test, y_all[te])
res$acc

# Accuracy per writer (the spread matters more than the average)
round(tapply(res$hat == y_all[te], y_all[te], mean), 2)

# Accuracy per digit
round(tapply(res$hat == y_all[te], meta$digit[te], mean), 2)
```
What the output shows

Per-writer accuracy varies enormously. It ranges from 0.00 to 1.00. One writer is recognised every time (1.00), three at 0.80, and two at 0.60. Two writers (labels 4 and 12) are never recognised, and several sit at 0.11-0.20.
Digits are about equal. Accuracy per digit is 0.34, 0.43, 0.36, 0.44 and 0.35, with no digit clearly easier. With about 20 test cells per digit, I wouldn’t read anything into the differences.
The labels are 0-19, not person_id. y_all was built as as.integer(person_f) - 1, so “writer 10” in this output is person_id 11. Add 1 when naming writers in the report, or relabel before printing.



```{r}
# Test loss and accuracy, as in the lecture
final %>% evaluate(x_test, y_test, verbose = 0)

# Confusion matrix (writers labelled by person_id)
pred_id <- as.integer(levels(person_f))[res$hat + 1]
conf <- table(true = meta$person_id[te], predicted = pred_id)
conf

# Easier to read: each row as proportions, with the diagonal being accuracy
round(conf / rowSums(conf), 2)
```
